answer.answer:
Moving fabrication off-site through prefabrication is the one directly evidenced route to improving site safety, and it is deployed today: several census-recorded processes were adopted specifically to address safety, mainly through material handling and surveying and mapping automation rather than by putting robots in harm's way on the structural site itself. If human-robot collaboration is used instead, safety depends on compliance with the ISO 10218 robot safety standard; this is a stated requirement, not an automatic outcome. Watch for the many risk factors that simply co-occur with the safety enabler rather than causing it: they signal contexts to check, not proven levers.

**The one directional path to site safety**: the evidence base contains a single dependency edge that leads into the "Improve site safety" enabler, and it runs from prefabrication. Prefabrication/off-site enables Improve site safety, because moving work offsite improves site safety. [1] This is backed by peer-reviewed evidence [DEP19]. The enabler itself is scoped to a specific stage of work: Enabler VA13 (Improve site safety) applies in the Structural Construction phase, with a value-realizing role there. [2] So the practical instruction is: shift as much structural-phase work as possible into off-site, factory-controlled prefabrication if site safety is the priority, rather than trying to re-engineer on-site robotic processes for the same end.

**Deployed cases adopted for safety**: four census records in this graph name safety explicitly as the reason for adoption, and they show what actually got automated. Case census_RX24 deployed a robotic construction process adopted to address safety, performing material handling, at technology readiness level 7. [3] Case census_RXM29-3 deployed a robotic construction process adopted to address safety, performing surveying and mapping, at technology readiness level 7. [4] Case census_RXM9-2 deployed a robotic construction process adopted to address safety, performing surveying and mapping, at technology readiness level 8. [5] Case census_RX48 deployed a robotic construction process adopted to address safety, at technology readiness level 6. [6] None of these four cases records a rationale of cost or quality, which distinguishes them from a case such as census_RXH9-3, whose deployed robotic construction process was adopted to address cost and quality, at technology readiness level 9 [7], not safety. In other words, if safety is the driver, the deployed pattern in this graph favours automating material handling, and surveying and mapping tasks, at TRL 6-8, over higher-maturity general deployment.

**If robots must work alongside people on-site**: the graph places a hard regulatory dependency here. Human-robot interaction depends on compliance with robot safety standards, meaning collaborative work is conditioned on meeting ISO 10218. [8] This is standard-grade evidence [DEP45], and it is echoed for bespoke fabrication technology more broadly: Bespoke DFAB technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance. [9] So any on-site or collaborative deployment needs ISO 10218-1/2 compliance built in from the start, not retrofitted.

**Related but not safety-specific dependencies to be aware of**: mobile, autonomously repositioning robots enable on-site digital fabrication (mobile robot with autonomous repositioning and localisation performs on-site digital fabrication [10], DEP86), and indoor site constraints limit localisation choices because reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, constraining path-planning localisation method choice [11] (DEP44). Neither of these is linked in this graph to the site-safety enabler directly; they are capability-enabling dependencies for on-site fabrication generally, and should not be read as safety interventions in their own right. Likewise, robotic assembly's productivity gain on geometrically complex walls (DEP95) is a time/efficiency amplifier, not a safety pathway.

**What to treat as correlation only**: the safety enabler co-occurs in the graph with a large number of risk factors (RI1 through RI20) and other value outcomes (VA14-VA25), but these are all marked as co-occurrence, not dependency, in the edge list. That means the graph does not support claiming any of these risk factors as a cause or a lever for safety; they are simply contexts observed alongside safety-motivated deployments, and should be investigated case by case rather than assumed
